guide-overview-text:
Eating well
A full stomach is not the same as a good diet

Every food now carries real-world nutrition: calories, fats, protein, carbohydrate and fiber, four fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K), vitamin C, the B vitamins, and three minerals (calcium, iron and potassium). Hold a food to see what one portion of it contains, or a bowl or pie to see what one serving contains, in grams and kcal (mg or mcg for vitamins and minerals).

Your body keeps a reserve of each of these fourteen nutrients. Eating fills them and everyday life uses them up. Open the character screen (characterdialog) to see them under Nutritional Reserves, where the five food group bars used to be. Each block on a bar is one day's worth, and hovering over a bar shows how much is stored, how many days it would last and what the nutrient does. Typing /nutrition in chat lists them all.

Fullness and calories
Fullness is how much your stomach holds, out of 300. It decides how much more you can eat, and it empties within 6 hours whatever you do. What keeps you alive is the calorie tank, shown by the bar next to your hotbar: it holds a week of hard work, digestion fills it and activity burns it. When it runs dry you start to starve. The other reserves show whether what you eat is any good. A stomach full of bread keeps you going, but it won't keep your vitamin C up.

While nutrient tracking is on, the five food group bars and the bonus health they gave are switched off, so only one nutrition system runs at a time. For now the other reserves only keep score; the effects of a good or poor diet will arrive in a later version.

Read on: digestion, nutrient reserves, how food is counted and what each nutrient does.
guide-reserves-text:
Nutrient reserves
Measured in days

Reserves are shown as amounts: kcal for calories, grams for fiber (and for the fats, protein and carbs in your gut), and mg or mcg for vitamins and minerals. The B vitamins are a mix of six, so they are shown in % of a day's need. Each reserve also says how many days it would last if you stopped eating that nutrient altogether; each block on its bar is one day.

To see every amount, in tooltips too, as % of a day's need instead, set DisplayUnits to "percent" in ModConfig/complexnutrition.json.

Daily needs
Calories 2,800 kcal for an active day, fats 80 g, protein 128 g, carbohydrate 300 g and fiber 30 g. Protein follows what an active person building strength eats, 1.6 g per kg of bodyweight for an 80 kg character, rather than the much lower food-label value. Vitamins and minerals use the adult daily values printed on real food labels: vitamin A 900 mcg, vitamin D 20 mcg, vitamin E 15 mg, vitamin K 120 mcg, vitamin C 90 mg, calcium 1,300 mg, iron 18 mg and potassium 4,700 mg.

Using it up
Vitamins, minerals and fiber each use up one day's worth per in-game day, awake or asleep. Calories burn with activity: standing still burns about 700 kcal a day and moving all day about 2,800, while sprinting, the cold and anything else that raises your hunger rate burn more. Fats, protein and carbohydrate are not stored here: they sit in your gut until they are digested into calories (see digestion). Nothing is used up in creative mode or while you are logged out.

How much the body can store
• Calories: up to 7 active days, 19,600 kcal, a store of body fat. A new character starts with 5 days' worth.
• Vitamins A, D, E and K: up to 25 days (22,500 mcg of vitamin A, for example). A new character starts with two weeks' worth, so running low takes a long time, and so does recovering.
• Calcium, iron and potassium: up to 10 days (180 mg of iron, for example). A new character starts with a week's worth.
• Vitamin C, B vitamins and fiber: 2 days at most (180 mg of vitamin C). A new character starts with one day's worth, so these are the first to run low.
Anything eaten past a full store is lost.

See also: digestion and how food is counted.
guide-counting-title: Complex Nutrition: How food is counted
guide-counting-text:
How food is counted
Every ingredient counts

Single foods
Each food has the weight of a real-world portion, and its nutrition comes from real food data for that weight. Spoiling food gives less fullness and fewer nutrients in the same measure; rot gives nothing. How full a food makes you follows its weight, not its calories (see digestion).

Meals
A serving from the cooking pot counts as the sum of its ingredients. Cooking makes food easier to digest but destroys some vitamins: a cooked meal gives about 20% more calories and carbohydrate, but half the vitamin C and three quarters of the B vitamins of its raw ingredients. Pickles and other crock contents count as they are.

Pies
A pie counts as its whole filling and crust, and each slice is a quarter of it. A charred pie has lost most of its value.

Drinks
Juice, milk and other drinkable liquids count by the litre, so a sip counts for a sip. Drinks fill you half as much as their weight would.

Large meals
The body can only take in so much at once. For fats, protein and carbohydrate this happens as they are digested: past a certain amount in a day, each extra gram gives fewer calories (see digestion). For fiber, vitamins and minerals, food eaten within an in-game hour of the last bite counts as one sitting. In one sitting, up to a day and a half's worth of each is taken in fully. Beyond that, each extra mouthful counts for less: a further full day's worth adds only about two thirds of a day. Spreading rich foods out, and eating a mix of them, works better than one big feast.

Mushrooms
Every mushroom species has its own profile. All are light, with few calories, but some are worth the hunt: morels are rich in iron, and chanterelles and morels carry vitamin D. The woody brackets (reishi, tinder hoof) are mostly fiber. Each mushroom weighs what its model suggests, and a patch drawn as a cluster drops several: a patch of morels or liberty caps gives four to eight small mushrooms, while a king bolete or an oyster gives one big one. Poisonous species still have their nutrients, and still poison you.

Foods from other mods
Foods without nutrition data of their own are estimated from their food group and vanilla satiety. Their tooltip says so.

See also: what each nutrient does.
guide-digestion-text:
Digestion
From stomach to calorie tank

Fullness
Your stomach holds 300 fullness, about a kilogram of food. Every food fills you by its weight: an apple fills 54, a loaf of bread 54, a whole cabbage 270. Meals, pies and anything cooked, baked, smoked or cured fill you 20% less, so cooking lets you eat more at once. Drinks fill half as much as their weight would, and porridge counts its cooking water. Fullness drains by 50 an hour, whatever you do, so a full stomach is empty in 6 hours. It only decides whether you can eat: something that does not fit has to wait, and an empty stomach does you no harm.

The gut
What you eat goes into your gut and is digested over hours. Each bite is digested evenly over its own time:
• Carbohydrate (not counting its fiber) in about 3 hours, up to 500 g at a time.
• Protein in about 6 hours, up to 200 g at a time.
• Fats in about 24 hours, up to 100 g at a time.
Anything past a full gut passes through unused. The Stats panel shows what is in your gut and how long it will take, and how much protein you took in over the last 24 hours, against the 128 g a day your body needs.

Calories
Digestion is the only thing that fills the calorie tank: 4 kcal for each gram of carbohydrate or protein and 9 for each gram of fats. The body only makes good use of so much: carbohydrate above 300 g in 12 hours, protein above 130 g in a day and fats above 70 g in a day each give fewer calories per extra gram. The tank holds 7 active days, and activity burns it. The bar next to your hotbar shows it, one block per day, and flashes when it falls below a tenth. When it is empty you starve, losing health until you eat. After dying you come back with at least a day's worth.

Fiber
With your fiber reserve at 70% of a day's need or more, digestion runs faster: fats 30%, protein 20% and carbohydrate 10%. The bonus shrinks as the reserve runs down. In real life fiber tends to slow digestion a little; here it is a reward for eating your greens.

What this means
A stomach full of stew gives about 1,000 kcal, a stomach full of bread over 3,000, and a stomach of mushrooms very little. Fruit and vegetables alone won't carry a hard-working day: add meat, grain, bread or cheese.

See also: nutrient reserves and how food is counted.
guide-nutrients-text:
The fourteen nutrients
What they do and where to find them

Only calories and fiber do something in game yet. Each of the others will get its own effect in a later version, even if a small one; until then, its entry below says In game: planned.

Calories: energy for everything you do. Your body makes them from fats, protein and carbohydrate. Densest in fat, butter, honey, nuts and bread. In game: an empty calorie tank starves you.
Fats: slow fuel, and needed to take in vitamins A, D, E and K. Animal fat, butter, walnuts, peanuts, cheese and sunflower seeds. In game: planned.
Protein: builds and repairs muscle. Meat, fish, cheese, soybeans and peanuts. In game: planned.
Carbohydrate: quick fuel. Grains, bread, honey and cassava. In game: planned.
Fiber: keeps digestion moving. Flax, rye, soybeans, peanuts and berries. In game: a good fiber reserve speeds up digestion, so calories refill faster.

Vitamin C: healing, and healthy gums. Sailors who went without it got scurvy. Blackcurrants, cloudberries, bell peppers, strawberries and oranges. Cooking destroys some of it. In game: planned.
B vitamins: turn food into energy. Meat, fish, soybeans, peanuts and sunflower seeds. In game: planned.
Vitamin A: eyesight and skin. Carrots, butter, pumpkin and cheese. In game: planned.
Vitamin D: strong bones, together with calcium. Smoked and cured fish, chanterelles, morels and eggs. In game: planned.
Vitamin E: protects the body's cells. Sunflower seeds, peanuts and olives. In game: planned.
Vitamin K: lets blood clot and wounds close. Cabbage, fennel, soybeans, parsnips, blackberries and blueberries. In game: planned.

Calcium: bones and teeth. Cheese, soybeans, milk and flax. In game: planned.
Iron: carries oxygen in the blood. Soybeans, morels, bushmeat, olives and amaranth. In game: planned.
Potassium: keeps muscles and nerves working. Soybeans, fish, cattail and papyrus roots, and peanuts. In game: planned.

See also: nutrient reserves.
